text: Logs, cost and latency dashboards, drift reports, hallucination scores — every one is pull-based. Alerting is what makes it push-based: the system notices and tells a person, instead of waiting for someone to notice.
An alert needs to be specific: a name, a metric — cost, error rate, token count — a numeric threshold that means something's actually wrong, and a time window that threshold applies over.

A rule that fires into a void is no better than no rule. A real system routes it somewhere a human will see it, with the exact metric, threshold, and which model violated it, plus a link back to the dashboard.
Once several alerts exist, the alerts list becomes its own thing worth watching — which are triggered, which are healthy, what each one actually checks.

It's tempting to alert on everything once the capability exists. But when every minor fluctuation triggers a notification, the team stops reading them, and the one alert that actually matters gets lost in the noise.
Chapter 3 built the full observability picture — logs, cost, drift, hallucinations, alerts. Chapter 4 turns to governance: bias, privacy, and compliance.
